title: 个, 本, 件: counting words
summary: Lets you count people and things with a number + counting word + noun, as in 三个人 and 两本书.
structure: Number + 个 / 本 / 件 + Noun
这 / 那 / 几 + 个 / 本 / 件 + Noun
explanation:
In English you can say "three friends" with nothing between the number and the noun. In Chinese you can't. You always need a small counting word in between. So "three friends" is 三个朋友, and "two books" is 两本书.

Each counting word goes with certain nouns. 个 is the most common one. Use it for people (人, 朋友, 学生) and for many everyday things (苹果, 问题). 本 is for books and other bound things (书, 汉语书). 件 is for clothes (衣服) and for matters or things to do (事). When you learn a new noun, learn its counting word with it.

You also need the counting word after 这 (this), 那 (that) and 几 (how many): 这本书, 那件衣服, 几个人. If everyone already knows what you mean, you can drop the noun: 我要两个 (I want two).

A common mix-up: for "two" before a counting word, say 两, not 二. So it's 两个人, never 二个人.

examples.en: This piece of clothing is very pretty.
How many Chinese books do you have?

examples.zh: 妈妈给我买了两件衣服。
examples.en: Mom bought me two pieces of clothing.

mistakes.why: A number can't go straight before a noun. You need a counting word in between, and for people it's 个.
Before a counting word, "two" is 两, not 二.
Books take the counting word 本, not 个.

why: Correct: people, like 朋友, are counted with 个.
本 is for books, not people.
件 is for clothes and matters, not people.
个 is very common, but books take their own counting word, 本.
Correct: 本 is the counting word for books.
件 is for clothes and matters, not books.

why: 几 also needs a counting word after it: 几本书.
Correct: 几 takes the place of the number, and 本 stays: 几本书.
Use only one counting word. 本 is enough, and adding 个 doubles it.
The order is 几 + 本 + 书, not 本 + 几.
